overview: This file assembles U.S. and British diplomatic and commercial reporting on Japan’s economy from mid-1930 to April 1932, documenting the effects of the global depression, deflation, the restored gold standard, unemployment, rural distress, collapsing silk markets, and government relief and domestic-products campaigns. Its detailed surveys cover foreign trade, fiscal and monetary conditions, transport, communications, commercial policy, and industries including silk, cotton, artificial silk, iron and steel, copper, cement, shipping, shipbuilding, and electric power. Reports on colonial Taiwan and Korea broaden the file’s scope to the economic organization of the Japanese Empire, while the final Embassy telegrams assess industrial finance, indebtedness, inventories, losses, and the budgetary consequences of the Manchurian Incident.
interest: The file is especially useful for tracing Japan’s movement from the deflationary crisis of 1930 to the fiscal and industrial pressures accompanying expansion in Manchuria by 1932. Its combination of broad British commercial handbooks, U.S. diplomatic observations, quantitative trade appendices, and rapid Embassy telegrams permits comparison between published surveys and confidential assessments. The inclusion of Taiwan and Korea also makes it valuable for studying Japan’s economy as an imperial system rather than solely as a national economy, while the industry-by-industry reports reveal how depression-era losses and debt were distributed across strategically important sectors.
